title: Science Connections: Find the Link
description: Can you find the hidden connections? Sixteen science terms are scrambled together -- group them into four categories before you run out of guesses. From chemical elements to planetary bodies, test your scientific knowledge by finding what links each set of four words together.
learning_objectives: Classify chemical elements by their properties and periodic table groups
Identify the major organ systems in the human body and their primary functions
Recall the planets of our solar system and distinguish their characteristics
Understand the four fundamental forces of nature and their roles in physics
Develop pattern recognition and categorical thinking skills in a scientific context

groups.label: Noble Gases (Group 18 Elements)
groups.explanation: Noble gases are the elements in Group 18 of the periodic table. They are characterised by their extremely low reactivity because they have a complete set of electrons in their outer shell. Helium is used in balloons, Neon in signage, Argon in welding, and Krypton in high-performance lighting.

groups.label: Human Body Systems
groups.explanation: The human body is organised into organ systems that work together to sustain life. The Circulatory system pumps blood, the Respiratory system handles breathing, the Digestive system processes food, and the Nervous system coordinates signals between the brain and the rest of the body.

groups.label: Inner Planets (Terrestrial Planets)
groups.explanation: The inner planets, also called terrestrial planets, are the four planets closest to the Sun. They are all rocky with solid surfaces, relatively small in size compared to gas giants, and have few or no moons. India's Mangalyaan mission successfully orbited Mars in 2014.

groups.label: Fundamental Forces of Nature
groups.explanation: Physics recognises four fundamental forces that govern all interactions in the universe. Gravity holds planets in orbit, the Electromagnetic force governs light and electricity, the Strong Nuclear force holds atomic nuclei together, and the Weak Nuclear force is responsible for radioactive decay. Indian physicist Satyendra Nath Bose's work on quantum mechanics contributed foundational insights to understanding these forces.

how_to_play.title: How to Play
steps: You will see 16 science-related words arranged in a 4x4 grid
Find groups of 4 words that share a common scientific connection
Select 4 words you believe belong together and tap 'Submit' to check your guess
If correct, the group is revealed with its category name, colour, and an explanation
You have a maximum of 4 incorrect guesses -- if you exceed this, the game ends
Try to find all 4 groups with the fewest mistakes to maximise your score
tips: Start with the group you are most confident about -- look for the easiest connection first
Watch out for words that could fit multiple categories -- for example, 'Mercury' is both a planet and an element
If you are stuck, try sorting words mentally into possible groups before committing
The colour-coded difficulty hints (easy to hard) can help you prioritise which groups to tackle first
Remember: Noble Gases are all on the far right of the periodic table, and Fundamental Forces are concepts from physics, not tangible objects

transfer_exercises.real_world: Making fast calls during a team project deadline crunch
transfer_exercises.challenge: Practice making a decision in under 60 seconds on something you've been procrastinating. Reflect on the outcome.

transfer_exercises.game_context: Recovering from mistakes in rapid gameplay
transfer_exercises.real_world: Bouncing back after a failed presentation or test
transfer_exercises.challenge: Write down one recent failure and three specific things you learned from it.

glossary_terms.definition: The mental effort required to process information and make decisions.
glossary_terms.example: Having too many options at once makes decisions harder and slower.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Working memory has limits. Experts chunk information into patterns, reducing cognitive load and enabling faster decisions.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Experienced doctors diagnose faster not because they think harder, but because they recognize patterns instantly.

glossary_terms.definition: Identifying recurring structures or relationships in information.
glossary_terms.example: Noticing that certain question types always have two plausible answers helps you focus faster.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Pattern recognition is a core skill in chess, medicine, engineering, and sport. It develops through deliberate practice.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Air traffic controllers recognize dangerous flight patterns faster than computers because of years of pattern training.

glossary_terms.definition: The ability to direct mental attention toward what matters most and ignore distractions.
glossary_terms.example: Under time pressure, completing questions you're confident about before tackling harder ones.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Focus is a trainable skill. The Pomodoro method, mindfulness, and deliberate practice all improve sustained attention.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Olympic athletes train mental focus as rigorously as physical skills — pressure performance depends on it.

coaching_moment: Notice how each decision here requires weighing multiple options. Strategic thinkers pause before choosing — what's the long-term implication of each answer?
cultural_context: Scientific literacy is a strategic priority under NEP 2020, which emphasises inquiry-based learning over rote memorisation. Science Connections: Find the Link builds the analytical instincts that support strong performance in India's science curricula.
reflection_prompt: What pattern did you start to recognize as you played? How will you use it next time?
